name: Malla kingdoms of Nepal
summary: The Malla dynasty ruled the Kathmandu valley, later split into three rival kingdoms whose Newar artists built the temples and palace squares still seen today; the Gorkha king Prithvi Narayan Shah conquered them in 1768–69.

knownFor.label: Durbar Squares
knownFor.note: Palace squares of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur.

location.value: The Kathmandu valley in central Nepal, with nearby hill lands.

terrain.value: A fertile lake-bed valley about 1,300 m high, ringed by the Himalayan foothills.

climate.value: Mild and subtropical, with a summer monsoon and cool, dry winters.

resources.value: Very fertile rice land, skilled craftsmen and control of trade routes to Tibet.

population.value: The page gives no population; a 1255 earthquake killed about one-third of Kathmandu’s people (30,000, including King Abhaya Malla).

urbanisation.value: Dense brick cities: Kathmandu (Kantipur), Patan (Lalitpur) and Bhaktapur, each with a royal palace square.

disease.value: Epidemics such as smallpox and cholera, and famines after poor harvests.

migration.value: Newar merchants and craftsmen settled in Lhasa and other Tibetan towns.

economicBase.value: Wealth came from trade: the valley stood at the departure point for two routes into Tibet, and Nepal gained the right to mint Tibet’s coins in the mid-17th century.

tradeRoutes.value: Mountain passes linking the Indian plains with Lhasa; Newar traders handled much of this trade.

wealth.value: Rich from trans-Himalayan trade, which paid for many temples and palaces.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver coins (mohars) minted in the valley were also used as currency in Tibet from the 1600s.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; some slavery or bonded labour.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy with no legislature; after 1482 the kingdom split into rival Kathmandu, Patan and Bhadgaon.

succession.value: Within branches of the Malla family; disputes led to the division of the kingdom.

institutions.value: Royal courts, Brahmin and Buddhist priests, and guthi trusts that ran temples, festivals and land.

eliteConflict.value: After 1482 the kings of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur competed and often fought.

armyAndTech.value: Small armies of local soldiers; the divided kingdoms could not stop the Gorkha army.

majorWars.value: Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha invaded in 1768–69, ending Malla rule in the valley.

territoryChange.value: Divided into three kingdoms after Yaksha Malla’s death (1482).

alliancesRivals.value: The three Malla kingdoms were rivals of each other; the Gorkha kingdom became the main threat.

inventions.value: No major inventions; Newar craftsmen were famous for metal casting and woodcarving.

scienceEducation.value: Sanskrit learning, copying of Buddhist and Hindu manuscripts, and astrology at court.

openness.value: Open to trade with Tibet and India and to Indian religious and court culture.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths and mountain trails; goods to Tibet were carried by porters and pack animals.

religion.value: Hinduism and Buddhism, with Buddhism a vital force especially in Patan; the Mallas also worshipped Kumari, a living goddess believed to be the reincarnation of Taleju.

languageWriting.value: Newar (Nepal Bhasa) and Sanskrit, written in Newar scripts; Maithili was used in court plays.

socialStructure.value: A caste order codified under Jayasthiti Malla (1380s), with Brahmins, merchants, farmers and craft castes.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Newar culture, language and festival calendar, with loyalty to each city’s king.

dailyLife.value: Multi-storey brick houses around courtyards; rice, festivals and guthi duties shaped the year.

neighbours.value: The Gorkha kingdom and other hill states, Tibet, and the kingdoms of the Indian plains.

ideasReligions.value: A blend of Hindu and Buddhist practice that is still central to Newar culture.

riseSignals.value: The Malla dynasty was founded by Arideva Malla, dated c. 1201 in the infobox.

peakPeriod.value: The page calls Yaksha Malla (c. 1428–82) the high point of the Mallas as rulers of a united Nepal and Pratap Malla (1641–74) the cultural high point of Kathmandu, so it differs from the entry’s 1600s.

declineSignals.value: Division into three kingdoms (1482) left them unable to resist Gorkha.

outcome.value: After Yaksha Malla’s death the valley was divided into Bhaktapur, Kantipur and Lalitpur; Prithvi Narayan Shah invaded in 1768–69 and the dynasty ended on 25 November 1769.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and foreign reports; figures are estimates.
